subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
subtype: Approach: private conversation with the manager first [Action]
passage:
I walked to Leela's cabin on a Tuesday afternoon with my heart going fast, and I had rehearsed the sentence the whole way. I'm Pooja.
"I saw the same delivery paid twice on the vendor sheet, Leela. Two invoices, same date, same amount. Can you help me understand it?" I kept my voice flat and did not say anything about what it might mean.
Leela looked at the sheet for a while. "That's the vendor sending a corrected copy. It should have been cancelled. Thank you for asking me first. I'll get finance to reverse it by Friday."
On Friday the second payment was reversed. I felt lighter than I'd expected, and a little silly for being so worried.
— Pooja

qa.q: What did Pooja notice on the vendor sheet?
qa.a: Pooja noticed the same delivery paid twice, with two invoices of the same date and amount.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling on the way to Leela's cabin?
qa.a: Pooja was nervous, with a fast-beating heart, and rehearsed the sentence the whole way.

qa.q: What could Pooja do if Leela had not explained or fixed it by Friday?
qa.a: Pooja could follow up in writing with the same facts and, if still unresolved, use the company's reporting route.

qa.q: How might Leela have felt hearing the concern in a private, calm way?
qa.a: Leela was probably grateful and not defensive, since Leela thanked Pooja for asking first and promised a fix.

grounding: The monologue shows an employee calmly telling a direct manager what was seen, asking for clarification and leaving room for an honest explanation or correction.

subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
subtype: Approach: escalating to compliance if unresolved [Revision]
passage:
Thursday night.
I talked to Tarun today, like I said I would. Calmly, with the dates: the same figures being changed before every month-end review. Tarun waved a hand. "Everyone does it. Don't make trouble." My cheeks were burning as I left the room.
I sat in the stairwell for a while. I wanted to vent in the team chat, or post something where people could see. I didn't. That feels like a different story from the one I want to tell.
Instead, I wrote a plain message to the compliance office: what I saw, on which dates, and that I raised it with Tarun first. Sent at 6:10. An acknowledgement with a reference number came within the hour.
Now I wait. I'm scared, but calm.
— Sarika

qa.q: What time did Sarika send the note to the compliance team?
qa.a: Sarika sent it at 6:10.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling after Tarun waved the concern away?
qa.a: Sarika felt embarrassed and shaken, with burning cheeks, and tempted to vent publicly.

qa.q: What could Sarika do if the compliance team does not respond?
qa.a: Sarika could quote the reference number and ask for an update, or use any other official channel the policy names.

qa.q: How might Tarun see Sarika's note to compliance?
qa.a: Tarun may feel surprised and worried that the concern went further, since Tarun had told Sarika not to make trouble.

grounding: The diary shows an employee whose manager dismisses a concern, so the employee sends a written note to the compliance team through the official process, without gossip.

subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
subtype: Approach: consulting a mentor outside the company [Action]
passage:
At the rice mill office in his small town, Tushar had noticed something in the weighing slips that troubled him, and he carried it for a week. Then on Sunday he took the local bus to see Minakshi, an old teacher's daughter who now worked at a firm in the next district.
Over tea at the bus-stand stall, he kept it general. "Suppose someone noticed figures that looked altered. How did you decide what to do in your job?"
Minakshi stirred her tea. "When it happened to me, I wrote down only what I had seen, read our policy and used the route it named. I never told anyone outside."
Tushar nodded. He had not said one name or number, and he felt steadier on the ride home.

qa.q: How did Tushar travel to see Minakshi?
qa.a: Tushar took the local bus.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling as he asked his general question?
qa.a: Tushar was uneasy and unsure, having carried the worry for a week, but relieved to be able to talk.

qa.q: What could Tushar do next after the talk with Minakshi?
qa.a: Tushar could read the mill's policy, write down what he saw with dates, and use the official route it names.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt hearing Tushar's question?
qa.a: Minakshi probably recognised the situation from her own experience and was glad to share what she had learned.

grounding: The passage shows an employee talking in general terms to a trusted mentor at another firm, learning how similar situations were handled, and revealing no confidential details.

subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
subtype: Approach: thinking through personal costs and protections [Thinking]
passage:
Subject: Thinking it through, and could you check my sums?

Dear Naveen,

You are the one person outside the office I trust to think this through with me. I have decided to report what I saw, but first I want to be clear about what it might cost.

Risks: my next promotion could stall, and if things turn ugly, my job could be at risk. I have read the protection section in our policy for people who report, and I will ask a lawyer to explain what the law says, since I don't want to guess.

Meanwhile I have set aside four months of costs and updated my CV, in case I need to look elsewhere.

Does that sound sensible to you?

Ishita

qa.q: How many months of costs has Ishita set aside?
qa.a: Ishita has set aside four months of costs.

qa.q: How does Ishita feel about reporting?
qa.a: Ishita is determined but careful, having decided to report while wanting to face the costs honestly, and asking a friend to check the plan.

qa.q: What could Ishita do if the lawyer says the protections are weaker than expected?
qa.a: Ishita could rethink the timing and the route of the report, and strengthen the savings and job search before going ahead.

qa.q: How might Naveen feel on receiving this email?
qa.a: Naveen probably feels trusted and a bit worried, and would likely reply thoughtfully since Ishita asked for a check.

grounding: The email shows an employee weighing career and financial risks, checking the company's protections for people who report, and planning savings and a job search in case of retaliation.

subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
subtype: Approach: rationalising the wrongdoing as common practice [Pitfall]
passage:
Month-end, Friday. In the sales office, Lokesh leaned over the desk. "Everyone rounds the figures up a bit, Seema. Nobody's hurt. It's how the game works." Seema had hesitated, then added a small amount to her own total. Nothing happened.
Three months later. The small amounts had grown, always "just to match last month". Seema's stomach twisted each time she pressed save, but the twist was getting weaker.
Quarter-end, Wednesday. The auditors asked why the figures did not match the bank records. Seema's name was on every changed sheet. Lokesh stared at his screen and said nothing. Seema was called into the manager's room, and the door closed behind her.

qa.q: Whose name was on every changed sheet?
qa.a: Seema's name was on every changed sheet.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling each time she pressed save in the second beat?
qa.a: Seema felt a twisting unease that was already growing weaker, as the habit made it seem normal.

qa.q: What could Seema have done in the first month when the rounding began?
qa.a: Seema could have refused to change the figures and asked the manager how totals should be recorded.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt when the auditors asked their questions?
qa.a: Lokesh was probably scared and wanted to avoid blame, as staring at the screen in silence suggests.

grounding: The passage shows an employee who copies colleagues' claim that everyone shaves numbers, so that small compromises grow until an audit shows a serious problem.

subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
subtype: Approach: leaving when the culture will not change [Revision]
passage:
Darshan had raised the concern three times: once in a team meeting, once in an email to the director, once in a quiet corner with the head of finance. Each time the answer was the same: "We'll look into it." Each time nothing changed.
On a Sunday evening in his Delhi flat, Darshan thought about the fourth time and realised it would not be a fourth attempt. It would be a decision to stay. "If I stay and say nothing, I'm part of it," he told himself.
He made a plan. He updated the CV, wrote to two former colleagues, and put a handover date on the calendar for after the current project. Then he met Vasudha, now at another firm, for coffee to ask what her workplace was really like.

qa.q: How many times had Darshan raised the concern?
qa.a: Darshan had raised it three times.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling on Sunday evening?
qa.a: Darshan felt frustrated and resigned, and was clear that staying silent would make him part of it.

qa.q: What could Darshan do while working out the notice period?
qa.a: Darshan could keep doing the work honestly, keep dated notes of the concerns raised, and prepare a clean handover.

qa.q: How might Vasudha see Darshan's questions about her workplace?
qa.a: Vasudha probably saw someone serious about finding values that match, and may have felt honoured to be asked for an honest picture.

grounding: The passage shows an employee whose repeated concerns are ignored, deciding that staying would mean joining the practice and starting a planned search for a workplace that fits.

subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: disclosing quickly and owning it [Action]
passage:
Tuesday, 10:42. Preeti ran a cleanup command, saw the screen scroll, and felt the blood leave her face. The customer table in the live system was gone. She had typed it in the wrong window.
Four minutes later Preeti was at Eshaan's desk. "I deleted the customer table on the live system. I ran the cleanup at 10:42 in the wrong window. Everything since last night's backup is missing, I think, and I don't know about anything else."
Wednesday. Eshaan's team restored last night's backup by noon and rebuilt the day's entries from the logs by evening.
Friday. In the review, Eshaan said, "You telling us in four minutes gave us the whole day. Tell us the same way next time."

qa.q: At what time did Preeti run the cleanup command?
qa.a: Preeti ran it at 10:42.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when she saw the screen scroll?
qa.a: Preeti felt shock and dread, as the blood left her face when she realised the table was gone.

qa.q: What could the team do to make sure a slip like this is caught earlier?
qa.a: They could add a confirmation step and separate windows for test and live work, so one wrong window cannot erase live data.

qa.q: How might Eshaan have felt when Preeti arrived at the desk?
qa.a: Eshaan was probably alarmed but grateful for the clear, immediate report, which let the team start work at once.

grounding: The passage shows an engineer who deletes a customer table by mistake, tells the lead within minutes with exact details and helps start recovery straight away.

subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: hiding the mistake and hoping it goes unnoticed [Pitfall]
passage:
Friday, evening.
The audit finished today. In March I typed the wrong tax rate into forty invoices. I didn't tell anyone. I opened each invoice and quietly changed it, no note, no reason. It took an evening, and I felt clever.
Today the auditors flagged edits with no explanation. Arnab, my manager, called me in. "Did you change these?" I said, "Yes, I fixed a typo." That wasn't the whole truth and Arnab knew it.
"The wrong rate," Arnab said, "I'd have fixed in a day. This I can't ignore." He didn't shout. That was worse.
I don't know if I'll get the same access again. I wish I'd walked to Arnab's desk in March.
— Hansa

qa.q: How many invoices did Hansa change quietly?
qa.a: Hansa changed forty invoices.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling while talking to Arnab?
qa.a: Hansa was ashamed and afraid, giving a half-truth and finding Arnab's quiet reaction worse than shouting.

qa.q: What could Hansa do now to begin rebuilding trust with Arnab?
qa.a: Hansa could give Arnab the full story, share a written account of every edit and offer to follow any check the team sets.

qa.q: How might Arnab have seen the hidden edits compared with the original mistake?
qa.a: Arnab saw the original mistake as easy to fix in a day, but the silent edits as a breach of trust that could not be ignored.

grounding: The diary shows an employee who quietly patches an error and says nothing, so that when an audit finds it later the concealment harms trust more than the mistake.

subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
passage:
Friday, 3:55 p.m. A script Devika had pushed that morning was overwriting product prices in the live shop. Devika read the alert once and said aloud, to nobody, "What else could go wrong from here?" The answer was on the screen: a sync job, set for six.
"Stop the schedule first," Devika said, and turned the sync off. "Then restore prices from this morning's backup. Then tell the customers who ordered."
Payal, from support, wrote a short note to the eleven affected buyers with the correct prices and an apology, and sent it by five.
Monday. The review started only after everything was fixed. Wednesday. The team talked about how the script had gone out without a check, without pointing fingers.

qa.q: How many buyers were told about the wrong prices?
qa.a: Eleven affected buyers were told.

qa.q: What was Devika probably feeling on reading the alert?
qa.a: Devika was alarmed but focused, asking what could still get worse instead of dwelling on blame.

qa.q: What could Devika do differently to catch a script like this earlier?
qa.a: Devika could have the script tested on a copy of the shop and reviewed by a colleague before it goes live.

qa.q: How might the affected buyers have seen Payal's note?
qa.a: The buyers would see a quick, honest correction with the right price, which builds more trust than silence.

grounding: The passage shows an employee containing damage first by asking what can still get worse, stopping the scheduled job, restoring a backup and informing customers, with blame left for later.

subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
passage:
The Thursday review room was quiet. Elizabeth sat at the far end with her laptop closed, shoulders hunched. She had been the one who ran the command that wiped the live data.
Ayesha, leading the meeting, wrote a question on the whiteboard: "Why did one command wipe the live data?" Then she turned to face the room. "Not who. Why does our set-up let a single person do this in one step?"
The list grew line by line. Everyone on the team had full delete rights. The test and live screens looked almost the same. Nothing asked, "Are you sure?" before the command ran.
Elizabeth looked up for the first time. "So it could have been anyone."
"Yes," Ayesha said. "Let's fix that."

qa.q: What did Ayesha write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: Ayesha wrote a question asking why one command wiped the live data.

qa.q: What was Ayesha likely feeling as she turned from the whiteboard to the room?
qa.a: Ayesha was calm and purposeful, wanting the team to look at the set-up instead of blaming a person.

qa.q: What could the team do next about the three gaps on the list?
qa.a: They could assign an owner and a date to each gap: limit delete rights, make test and live look different, and add a confirmation step.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth have felt when the list showed it could have been anyone?
qa.a: Elizabeth probably felt relief and less alone, shown by looking up for the first time after sitting hunched.

grounding: The passage shows a team asking why the set-up allowed one command to remove live data and finding weak permissions, similar-looking screens and no confirmation step.
